content: You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition? Launching AI in English is fast, but it ignores a massive global market. To earn your next million users, look beyond simple translation. Copied to clipboard  		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 Many AI startups launch first in English because the models, benchmarks, developer tools and enterprise buyers are easiest to find there. That approach can help a company reach the market quickly, but it can also cause founders to overlook a much larger multilingual opportunity. According to the International Telecommunication Union, 2.2 billion people remained offline in 2025, most of them in low- and middle-income countries. As more of these users come online, many will expect digital products to work in the languages they use every day — not merely offer translated versions of English-first experiences. They represent a significant growth opportunity for companies prepared to build multilingual products. But founders cannot simply plug a translation API into an English-based model and instantly go global. Many general-purpose models provide uneven performance across languages. Some languages are represented by more tokens for equivalent content, which can increase cost and reduce the effective amount of text that fits into a context window. Lower-resource languages may also receive weaker results because they have less high-quality training and evaluation data. I have seen this challenge firsthand through my contributions to the Government of India’s BHASHINI and BhashaDaan initiatives and as an expert contributor to C-DAC’s Vikaspedia. BhashaDaan crowdsources speech, text, translation and image-labeling contributions for Indian-language technologies, while Vikaspedia provides knowledge across social-development sectors in India’s scheduled languages. Contributing to these initiatives reinforced a consistent lesson: You cannot serve a multilingual market by treating language support as a translation feature added at the end. “Tokens” are the fundamental billing unit of generative AI. Tokenization varies by model, and even English words do not always map to one token. However, multilingual studies have found that equivalent content can require materially different numbers of tokens across languages. When a tokenizer fragments a target language more heavily, the application may pay for more input and output tokens to communicate the same meaning. A simple first estimate is: Estimated multilingual text cost = Comparable English text cost × Token-count multiplier. This estimate does not include differences in model pricing, caching, output length or infrastructure. A language-focused tokenizer or model may materially reduce inference costs, but founders should benchmark it using representative conversations in each target language before making a platform decision. Engineering teams should compare general-purpose and language-focused models using representative regional inputs. Evaluate token count, response quality, latency, safety, licensing and total cost together. A model that uses fewer tokens is not a better business choice if it produces less reliable answers. High-quality digital and training resources are distributed unevenly across languages, leaving many lower-resource languages with less material for model training, retrieval and evaluation. When startups implement Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for regional languages, their systems may produce weaker or less grounded results when suitable localized retrieval and evaluation data is sparse, outdated or poorly translated. Founders should evaluate sovereign and institutional language resources before paying to recreate equivalent data. Before using any resource for retrieval, fine-tuning or commercial deployment, verify its license, provenance, update history, quality, privacy conditions and permitted uses. Government backing should not replace technical and legal due diligence. Properly licensed, relevant resources can improve language coverage and reduce the amount of data a startup must collect independently, but their quality and suitability must still be tested. When building for the U.S. enterprise market, the default user interface is often a text box and a keyboard. However, mobile-internet research indicates that reading, writing and digital-literacy difficulties are major barriers to mobile-internet adoption. In markets where user research identifies typing, literacy or script entry as meaningful barriers, founders should evaluate voice-enabled and visual interfaces rather than assuming that a text box is sufficient. As I explained in my earlier analysis of conversational AI and “Zero-UI” systems, reaching the next billion users often requires fitting technology into their existing communication habits rather than forcing them to navigate a conventional app If voice is central to the target workflow, design and test the audio pipeline early. It should be evaluated using representative accents, dialects, noisy environments and code-mixed speech rather than added as an untested wrapper at launch. Multilingual expansion should also begin with one narrowly defined market rather than a simultaneous global launch. Choose a high-value workflow, test it with native speakers, measure task completion and support costs, then use that evidence to decide whether the architecture is ready for the next language. Multilingual markets contain users whose needs are poorly served by English-first products. Capturing this opportunity requires treating localized AI as a core engineering and product discipline. Audit your token economics to protect your margins, verify the legal and technical quality of regional datasets and design interfaces around how target users actually communicate. An English-only architecture may prevent an otherwise strong AI company from reaching users who prefer to speak, search and transact in other languages. Many AI startups launch first in English because the models, benchmarks, developer tools and enterprise buyers are easiest to find there. That approach can help a company reach the market quickly, but it can also cause founders to overlook a much larger multilingual opportunity. According to the International Telecommunication Union, 2.2 billion people remained offline in 2025, most of them in low- and middle-income countries. As more of these users come online, many will expect digital products to work in the languages they use every day — not merely offer translated versions of English-first experiences. Over 20 years of combined experience and the latest in technology, AI,… North Carolina recorded its 12th consecutive month with more than $500 million wagered on sports, extending a run that signals sustained market activity while counselors warn about gambling addiction. The milestone was reported by Spectrum Local News on Friday, October 2. The outlet’s report also examined concerns about the effects of betting, particularly on young adults, and whether the state’s support for people experiencing gambling problems is adequate. North Carolina bettors wagered $520.5 million in August 2026, an 8.5% increase from August 2025, according to the Winston-Salem Journal. The figure made August the 12th straight month above the half-billion-dollar threshold. Eight sportsbooks were operating in the state that month. The Journal also reported that $7.82 billion was wagered during fiscal 2025-26, up 14.9% from $6.63 billion in fiscal 2024-25. Those figures offer a wider view of the market’s scale, beyond the monthly streak. Legal mobile sports betting began in North Carolina on March 11, 2024. The state’s tax rules are part of the operating environment for sportsbooks, with North Carolina’s sports-betting tax framework shaping the market alongside continuing bettor demand. The Spectrum report centered on counselors’ concern that sports betting can become harmful, including for emerging adults. Dr. Jessica Auslander, a sports gambling counselor, said most of her new client inquiries over the previous year or so were related to sports betting. She identified an emerging adult aged 18 to 24 as the most common client profile lately. Warning signs can include being unable to stop placing bets, spending excessive time researching them, irritability and withdrawing from others. The report also described concerns about betting products that may introduce younger people to wagering habits before they are old enough to use legal sportsbook apps. North Carolina law directs $2 million each year from digital sports-betting tax proceeds to the Department of Health and Human Services for gambling-addiction education and treatment. Morgan Coyner, executive vice president of the Addiction Professionals of North Carolina, said the amount is not enough to address a growing problem. The question of whether funding keeps pace with the market’s scale has also featured in discussion of North Carolina’s sports-betting tax revenue. A survey of North Carolina residents conducted this summer with Meredith College found that three-quarters of respondents supported using mobile sports-betting taxes to fund research on problem gambling. The same survey found that 67% supported legislation to ban prediction markets, a separate policy question raised in the report. The results show the public-health debate running alongside the betting figures: sustained wagering brings commercial scale, but also pressure to decide whether existing prevention and treatment measures are sufficient. The month-by-month streak marks a consistent level of activity; it does not, by itself, answer how the state should respond to the risks counselors describe. Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, said applying the full $5,000 penalty to the number of violations would create too large of a penalty under the US Constitution's protections on due process. I ass/u/me this refers to the Eighth Amendment, but I don't remember seeing any monetary constants encoded within that text. Google's telling me Meta is worth about $1.8 trillion so how would a mere $40B be "excessive?" It's only about 2% of their worth! Civil penalties in excess of 2% of someone's worth are routinely accepted as constitutional, aren't they? If this case were about me driving drunk and killing a whole family, I bet no one would flinch at the 8A implications of taking 2% (!?!) of my assets, and everyone would laugh at my lawyer if he brought up 8A for such an insignificant fine. I understand why we have 8A, and everyone deserves mercy, but I don't see why Meta deserves exceptional mercy as a singular special case that we would be horrified to see applied anywhere else. Bringing up 8A for such a tiny fine would be giving Meta a very unique carve-out that we normally would not apply. It may be that $5k is too much to charge criminals per act, in that each crime didn't really cause that much loss, but bringing up due process concerns seems like bullshit when the fine is already so small. NM and Meta had been trying to negotiate the cost of illegal business for years before negotiations failed and it went to trial. Meta decided to let a jury decide, and the jury's come up with a fairly tiny fraction of their assets. If Meta thinks the price of illegal business is still too high, then they can lower the number of willful violations they commit per year, to optimize the advantage they gain from illegal actions at an affordable rate. Geez, Zuck, just do less of it. If $40B seems like a lot, then maybe try only $10B worth of crime next time. What's the big deal? Live and learn. After this little fine you still have 98% of the company left to go on and incur the next wave of liabilities. Cruel and Unusual punishment includes excessive fines. The question becomes "What constitutes an excessive fine?"The answer is "A fine that is not in keeping with what others have been fined for similar violations." We know what other fines have been levied in the past, but what constitutes a "similar violation"?If there is not a clear answer, then it becomes a matter of "What fines were levied against other big companies?" This is what gets argued on appeal. "Was the violation similar?  In scope if not type?  There may be more comments in this discussion. Over 20 years of combined experience and the latest in technology, AI,… New York has moved to sue Polymarket as prediction markets offer sports contracts outside the state’s sportsbook tax framework, raising questions about a gambling-tax base worth more than $1 billion a year. The platforms argue that they operate as federally overseen derivatives exchanges, not under state gambling laws, a dispute that could shape where sports-related wagering is taxed. The conflict puts a large revenue stream in focus. New York’s legal and tax treatment of prediction-market contracts is also part of a broader debate over whether these products compete with licensed sportsbooks. Mobile sports betting generated about $328 million in tax receipts for New York in the first quarter of 2026, according to the state comptroller’s office. New York accounts for roughly one-third of all state tax collections on sports-betting revenue nationwide, while licensed sportsbooks face a 51% state tax rate. A Tax Policy Center analysis estimates that if 1% of New York sportsbook activity shifted to prediction markets, the state could lose $13 million in revenue. That is a modeled estimate, not evidence that the shift has already happened. Polymarket and Kalshi have added sports-related contracts, giving customers another way to trade on sporting events. Federally regulated prediction-market exchanges could compete with licensed sportsbooks while operating under a different regulatory framework. That distinction is central to the competition between prediction markets and sportsbooks, but the potential tax impact depends on whether customers actually move their activity. DraftKings has offered one early indication that the audiences may differ: a company spokesperson said about 1% of its sportsbook customers overlap with Kalshi in states where sports betting is legal. That customer-overlap figure is separate from the Tax Policy Center’s estimate, which models a 1% shift in sportsbook activity across New York. Kalshi disputes that its growth is taking revenue from traditional sportsbooks. Company spokesperson Dani Lever said, “We can operate under federal regulation while continuing to generate vital tax revenue for states.” Prediction-market operators maintain that federal oversight applies to their exchanges rather than state gambling laws; New York’s position puts that claim in direct tension with the state’s tax system. Maria Doulis, New York State deputy comptroller for budget and policy analysis, said, “For a user, it’s not clear that engaging in activity on a prediction market is a substantially different activity than placing a wager on a mobile sports betting platform,” and added, “But from the state’s perspective, those two activities are taxed differently and can yield two different outcomes.” Kalshi’s trading volume rose nearly thirteenfold in the year after it added sports contracts. Polymarket also saw rapid growth after adding sports, according to a New York State Comptroller report. Those figures indicate expanding activity, but do not establish how much-if any-came from customers leaving state-licensed sportsbooks. The fiscal stakes extend beyond tax receipts. Calls to New York’s gambling hotline have risen 8.5% since 2020, and the state has doubled funding for problem-gambling services, from $6 million to $12 million. Prediction markets’ growth could add to the state’s policy challenge if more gambling activity shifts beyond its existing framework. Sportsbook revenue can fluctuate even without competition from prediction markets. The New York Knicks’ NBA Finals win, after entering the series as underdogs, led mobile sportsbooks to lose $14.4 million in gross revenue. Doulis said volatility-or a surge in prediction markets that affects sports-betting revenue-could have implications for state finances. New York has not identified a hearing, deadline or other procedural next step in the account of its move against Polymarket. The unresolved question for the state is whether prediction markets can keep expanding without diverting enough sportsbook activity to make the tax impact more than a projection. Tech > Mobile If you're eligible to receive payment in the class-action settlement surrounding Apple's AI lawsuit, the claims website is now live. Senior Writer Senior Writer October 3, 2026, 8:23 am ET Apple is settling a lawsuit related to the delayed rollout of Apple Intelligence features. Apple’s legal settlement over its allegedly misleading AI claims during the initial Apple Intelligence launch has finally reached the point where you can sign up to be paid from the $250 million pool via a live website. Apple settled a false advertising lawsuit brought by Clarkson Law Firm in May, agreeing to pay $250 million to customers who bought some iPhone models during a specified period. The lawsuit alleged that Apple misled customers by promising AI features that didn’t ship with the new devices. If you purchased an iPhone 16 or iPhone 15 at launch, you may be entitled to receive a portion of the quarter-billion-dollar settlement. Payouts between $25 and $95 per eligible device are expected. “Apple has reached a settlement to resolve claims related to the availability of two additional features. We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users,” an Apple spokesperson said in an earlier statement to CNET. The court granted preliminary approval of the settlement on July 17. Then an Aug. 13 order moved up the final approval date by seven months. Apple lit up its flagship New York City store to resemble Siri’s new color scheme. As of Sept. 21, you can go to SmartphoneAISettlement.com and enter your information to confirm your eligibility for monetary relief. People whom Apple and the settlement administrator determined would be eligible will also receive email or postal notices from the company Verita directing them to the website. The claims window closes on Dec. 21, 2026, so you have three months to act.  If you bought one of the following devices between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, you could be eligible to receive a settlement payment: The iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max are included because they have the processor and memory to run Apple Intelligence features. It’s estimated that approximately 36 million customers are eligible for this settlement. When Apple advertised its new iPhone 16 lineup in 2024, it emphasized how the models were optimized for AI features such as an enhanced Siri that could act as an intelligent agent. When the phones did arrive, Apple Intelligence wasn’t yet ready; its first features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, five weeks later. According to the proposed settlement, “Apple allegedly saturated the market with deceptive ads, inducing consumers to purchase iPhones based on the promise of certain enhanced Siri features.” Some features of Apple Intelligence did ship soon after the introduction of the iPhone 16 and iOS 18, including Visual Intelligence, Live Translation, Writing Tools, Genmoji and Clean Up. But those weren’t the advanced features Apple highlighted. In fact, the type of intelligent interactions Apple advertised is only starting to show up in Siri AI, which is part of iOS 27, which was released in early September. According to the settlement, Apple needed to provide the information about affected customers within five days of the settlement approval. As of late July, preliminary approval has been granted by the court. After the data is provided and verified, a 45-day notice period begins to inform potential consumers that they’re eligible for a payment. On Aug. 13, US District Court Judge Noël Wise granted approval to push forward the date from Sept. 29, 2027, to Feb. 24, 2027. Provided approval is granted, the first checks or deposits will arrive sometime within a 60-day window after February next year, depending on court dates and possible extensions.   		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. Many Americans are bristling over the data center buildout. Reid Hoffman says he's thankful for it. The LinkedIn cofounder said so during an appearance on the "Newcomer" podcast that was released Friday. Hoffman credited the huge amount of capital behind the AI infrastructure buildout for being "the only reason we're not in a recession." He said "most of that capital" doesn't go to the areas where data centers are being built. "Most of that's more distributed across the country," he said. "That's great." Hoffman said that in addition to powering the AI boom, data center construction also provides work for construction workers, electricians, carpenters, real estate agents, and lawyers. "All of this capital infusion, people think, 'Oh, that's just going to the tech companies,'" he said, adding that a "massive percentage of it is going towards data center construction." Data centers have recently emerged as a source of bipartisan fury as midterm elections approach. Both Republican and Democratic governors have recently moved to curtail or restrict construction. In a poll released last week by the Pew Research Center, which surveyed people in August, half of rural Americans said data centers "are mostly bad for the environment" — a figure substantially higher than in January, when it sat at 32%. At the same time, US investors have mind-boggling amounts of money riding on the hope that AI will soon become profitable. Data centers will play a key role in that. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    And for AI companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, and others, the issue is existential. Without AI data centers, they can't power the products they sell. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has recently suggested that new data centers could be built far from where people live, such as in the desert. For Hoffman, the issue is simple: Data center builders need to work fairly with local communities to ensure that both sides get a good deal, he said. As for his recession statements, the US economy is still on solid ground, even outside the blistering pace of tech capital expenditures. Despite a disappointing September jobs report, unemployment remained low, suggesting a middling rather than a recessionary labor market. And, overall, economic growth is still strong. Real gross domestic product grew at a 2.2% annual rate in the second quarter; that measure typically declines during recessions. Real personal income minus transfers, another recession indicator, is also up from a year ago, and consumer spending is still growing.       No comments right now, check back later. AIDonald TrumpNvidiaRTX 5090  The AI race has bodied the market for high performance computer hardware. As data centers lock in as much gear as possible, it has left the rest of the world paying premiums on tech that was trending towards affordable just a few years ago. How far buyers are willing to be pushed is yet to be fully tested. One enthusiast in California has raised concern over a loyalty pledge they were asked to sign to buy an Nvidia RTX 5090, promising not to flip the hardware and tying the purchase to government ID. “Picked up a Powerspec Ai90 prebuilt PC with a RTX 5090 in it,” posted Reddit user Krothic. “Apparently the manager required me to fill out this form and scan my driver license. Said it was a new thing starting just about two days ago. Had no problem doing so but thought it was interesting.” Krothic purchased their RTX at a Micro Center in Tustin, California. According to the post, the store had them sign a declaration in order to make the purchase. The single page form asks that the buyer guarantee the card will be used for personal or business use, and moreover that it won’t be resold or even given away. The pledge puts a hard emphasis on nationality as well, demanding that the card remain in the United States. The form asks to list a home address, government issued ID and the intended use of the hardware. What the penalties are for breaching the contract is unclear, but having the device tied to oneâs ID would make it easy to trace if caught. In the comments, others sound off on similar scrutiny at other stores, the top comment saying they were grilled by a manager to prove their gamer bonafides (with photo evidence). Others believe the document was spurred by resale value for RTX cards internationally and recent policies from Washington banning consumer GPUs from being exported to countries like China. While Trumpâs chosen nomenclature for âSuper Intelligenceâ is still taking shape, itâs clear that his administration is infatuated with the AI space. Against the tide of dissatisfaction, the White House is pushing for data center construction and further development of LLMs. As much as AI has grown in North America, itâs exploded across Asia, with Chinaâs industry among the fastest growing. Whether for information security or more literal warfare, it seems Washington wants to prevent hardware from freeing up to other countries. It is likely that retailers like Micro Center are reacting to these new pressures, and that other stores may have to exercise their own measures as well. Itâs not the first time Trump policy has had strange repercussions in the gaming space, and AIâs warpath in general has drastically inflated prices on PC and console hardware alike. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple. MacPaw spent nearly two decades building consumer software for Mac users. CleanMyMac is one of the Mac utilities on the market, and it’s my go-to when I need to free up hard drive space, uninstall apps, etc. The company is making a different kind of bet with Leebry, a Work AI platform aimed at helping IT teams. About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments. MacPaw’s 2026 AI at Work report is where you see the issue IT faces, as they found that 90% of companies deploy AI without thoroughly auditing their internal knowledge base first. That means that internal AI tools are answering employee questions based on whatever it can find, including old product docs, outdated policies, and random Reddit discussion forums. In this survey, MacPaw found that 6 in 10 IT leaders see a real disconnect between what their C-Suite expects from AI tools (thanks to LinkedIn feeds) and what their teams can safely and accurately deliver. That gap is where most AI disappointment lives, and it’s the problem Leebry is attempting to solve for IT teams. Leebry began as an internal MacPaw hackathon project in 2025. The problem it was solving was employees repeatedly asking the same questions internally, even when the answers already existed somewhere in the company’s documentation, intranets, Slack threads, etc. MacPaw built a Slack bot to surface those answers and point employees to the exact source. Within a few months, it was resolving 30% of MacPaw’s own level 1 IT tickets, so that became the foundation for what they’re launching today with Leebry. The platform automates level 1 support tickets, handles access provisioning and removal as employees join, move roles, or leave, and answers employee questions across the tools they already use. Every Leebry response links back to its source, so employees can verify the answer rather than just trust it (and prove it), and can flag stale or outdated information that could affect accuracy. That last part is the direct product response to the 90% knowledge audit problem from their own research. One detail worth calling out for security-conscious IT folks: Leebry is permission-aware, meaning it authenticates each user and surfaces only the information they are permitted to see. That matters more than it sounds as a lot of AI tools draw on a shared knowledge pool and let users surface things they shouldn’t access. Leebry also ships with an MCP server that exposes the device management control plane to AI agents, with admin-set guardrails on every action, so teams can delegate repetitive work to agents without giving up control over what those agents can actually do. For IT orgs that work extensively with Apple, the access provisioning aspect is interesting. Automating access changes as people move within the organization can be a huge pain point for SMBs without a dedicated IAM team. Most of the time, it’s manual, it’s slow, and departing employees end up with access that should have been revoked days earlier. I’ve run into this myself quite a bit. “Businesses don’t need another tool to check, they need work taken off their plate, without sacrificing oversight or control,” said Dan Jaenicke, Director of B2B Product Development at MacPaw. The fair question here is why an IT team should trust a consumer Mac software company to build enterprise tooling. I think the answer is actually in the product’s origin story. MacPaw built Leebry to solve their own internal IT problem first, which is a better foundation than most enterprise software gets. It wasn’t built to make money. It was built to solve a customer (even internal) problem, so it’ll work well for other teams. The reality is all orgs have docs spread out across team chat, file sharing, intranets, etc and we’re all guilty of asking for someone else to find it for us. The N100 mini PC has been an automatic recommendation for home lab use since it was introduced, and it earned that spot legitimately. It's low power with cores powerful enough to run a decent collection of services on, and it doesn't cost a fortune to leave running 24/7. It's still a good mini PC, but if you're entering into the market today and looking for something brand-new, the N150 costs about the same. Just don't overpay for it, because the N100 is still a worthy node in many respects. Especially for hardcore tinkerers  The N100 was basically as entry-level as it got when it came to a small form-factor PC. A Beelink Mini S12 Pro with 16GB of RAM and 500GB of solid-state storage used to routinely drop to around $170, but now, that configuration is over twice the price on Amazon. Other N100s have had similar jumps in price, and that flattens the difference between the generations. The N150 can easily be found for around the same price, plus or minus a few bucks. Beelink's N150-based EQ14, also with 16GB and 500GB of storage, is $385 on the company's store. When memory and storage make up so much of the bill, the processor doesn't move the needle on price much, and that makes the old chip not as much of a bargain anymore. Proxmox is in a league of its own when it comes to home lab projects  The silicon is one thing, but the manufacturers of these mini PCs have changed their designs according to the market that uses these things the most, and that happens to be home lab enthusiasts. The aforementioned EQ14 has a built-in power supply, two M.2 slots, and two Ethernet ports, with an option for dual Intel 2.5GbE. Looking at some of the other popular options, the Beelink ME mini fits six M.2 slots, dual 2.5GbE, and an internal power supply into a 99mm cube, CWWK's P6 pairs the N150 with four NVMe slots and a DDR5 SO-DIMM slot, and HUNSN sells fanless N150 appliances with four 2.5GbE ports for firewall duty. For a Proxmox node, an OPNsense box, or a small all-flash NAS, port count and storage layout decide what the machine can do, and a small bump in clock speeds or efficiency doesn't do much. Plenty of N100 machines offered similar layouts but the refreshed and newly designed models are shipping with the N150 at the same price. My ol' gaming rig still chugs along with the rest of my computing arsenal The N100 and N150 are quite close to each other, and calling it a generational leap would be seriously overselling the difference between them. The N150 is the N100 with the turbo ceiling raised from 3.4GHz to 3.6GHz and the integrated graphics clock raised from 750MHz to 1GHz. It has the same four efficiency cores, the same 6W base power, the same 24 execution units, and the same Quick Sync support. If I were to run the same set of containers on both systems, you wouldn't notice the difference between them at all. A mini PC might not beat a desktop, but for some gamers, it might prove to be the better gaming device  The difference between the N100 and the N150 in terms of performance is negligible for most home lab uses, so if you can find either for a decent price, it's worth pulling the trigger on. The older processor is just as capable as the newer one with very little separating them. If you're not willing to pay the inflated prices for either box at retail, the best move would be to try and find a pre-owned N100 on the used market, but that's easier said than done for a multitude of reasons. The first being that these boxes aren't something users will upgrade from much, if at all. The N100 is really capable still, and home lab enthusiasts are resourceful people—if it no longer fits the bill for the initial deployment, it's extremely likely that they'll find another use for it somewhere in their home before they turn to selling it. Find someone who runs a home lab, and I'll show you a tech hoarder. The second problem follows the first: because home labbers are less likely to let go of their N100s, the ones that do hit the market are at inflated prices. These are users that bought it when it was under $200 and can easily sell it for above that, especially on an auction site where they can set the minimum price higher than what they paid at retail. The N150 isn't Intel's newest budget chip, either. Wildcat Lake boxes like Beelink's EQ mini and EQi start $45 to $85 higher and add a performance core and 10GbE, so if your budget stretches and your workload can saturate it, it's worth picking up. My energy bills would hit the red zone without these tweaks The N100 earned its reputation for all the right reasons, and almost all of that can also be passed along to its successor, the N150. If you already own one, there's no point in upgrading, but if you're in the market for a mini PC to add to your home lab as a node, the N150 is a great choice for all of the same reasons as the N100 was, just don't overpay for it. Etihad Airways is bringing a new aircraft to its fleet in 2027, and I got an early look at what its premium seats will be like. At Dubai's annual Arabian Travel Market trade show in September, the UAE airline unveiled mock-ups of the new first- and business-class cabins planned for its future Airbus A330neos. Etihad said the first of 15 new A330neos will enter service in September 2027, serving regional and medium-haul routes from its Abu Dhabi hub.  There are just four first-class suites, followed by 24 business class seats. Both cabins have privacy doors, lie-flat seats, 4K screens, Bluetooth connectivity, and wireless charging. It's notable that Etihad is continuing to expand First beyond its flagship Airbus A380s. The choice makes sense, as the post-COVID premium travel boom continues to drive global airline revenue. Sitting inside the future A330neo cabins revealed much about how Etihad maximized space, as well as a few trade-offs that weren't immediately apparent. Here are eight things that stood out most. Once I sat down, the suite felt surprisingly spacious for everything Etihad packed around me. The leather felt premium, the finishes weren't tacky, and the different materials worked well together. It still felt roomy amid the screen, companion seat, console, and privacy walls. The seat didn't feel dramatically larger than some business-class cabins I've flown, though. Sitting in it reminded me of Gulf Air's Boeing 787 Apex Suite. The 32-inch 4K screen dominates the First suite, fully occupying the space in front of it. Its minimal borders make it appear larger, almost like having a miniature movie theater. One listed feature I appreciated in both new premium cabins was Bluetooth connectivity. It would allow me to pair my own noise-canceling headphones with the entertainment system. That said, business class' 17.3-inch screen felt noticeably compact after experiencing First's massive display. Etihad's first and business cabins had sleek control panels integrated beside the seat. There are settings for lighting, seat positions, and privacy. Wireless charging, TV controls, and headphone storage were all within easy reach. The mock-ups also had a 60-watt USB-C and a 110-volt universal power outlet. There was also a second control panel beside my hip when I laid flat. Etihad promotes the buddy seat in First for dining or socializing. I immediately saw another use: Working face-to-face with a colleague. Though with limitations. At 161 centimeters tall, my legs already extended well into the space between us. Put two 180-centimeter passengers opposite each other, and I expect their knees would become well acquainted. I couldn't test the dining table, so I'd wonder whether two laptops or full meals actually fit.  Also, both people need to be traveling in First Class. Etihad said travelers in Business or Economy could not join them, telling me: "Cross-cabin guests are not allowed." I would've missed the drawer Etihad calls the "personal powder room," had I not known about it. Despite the name, it isn't a separate room. It's a deep vanity compartment with a mirror and space for toiletries. During the walkthrough, Etihad shared that first-class passengers will also receive a Giorgio Armani amenity kit with ESPA skincare, premium loungewear, slippers, and a full turndown service. Meanwhile, business-class passengers receive a different amenity kit with LaNeige skincare, while loungewear and slippers are available on longer flights. Lying flat with the manual privacy door closed, the rest of the cabin almost disappeared from view. In both cabins, I couldn't see over the walls or through obvious gaps. My head and feet didn't feel exposed, making the seat feel like my own room in the sky. The divider behind First made the cabin feel separate while I was sitting inside my suite. Walking out told a different story. The four first-class suites sit directly ahead of business class. One step took me from First into the next cabin. An Etihad representative confirmed to me that first and business are physically connected. I'm used to premium cabins with clearly defined sections and physical separation, so the transition surprised me. That's one of the trade-offs to squeezing first class into the smaller widebody. Business was already configured as a bed when I climbed in, giving me a chance to see where its smaller footprint became noticeable. At my height, I fit comfortably with plenty of headroom. There was less open space toward my feet, with the space extending beneath the screen. That contrast ultimately summed up both cabins for me. First uses its extra space to create something akin to a private room, while business-class borrows similar features into a more compact suite. A few minutes inside a mock-up can't replicate several hours in the air. But sitting inside both cabins showed me far more than renderings or measurements could. Still, these upgraded premium cabins will likely come at a steep price. In April, a round-trip first-class ticket from New York to Abu Dhabi on Etihad's Boeing 787, which features one of Etihad's newer cabin products, costs about $6,000, versus roughly $3,800 in business class and $400 in economy. For years, Subway felt like the only relevant sandwich chain. Its 2008 "five, five dollar, five dollar footlong" jingle still lives in my head. The Connecticut-founded fast-food giant operates over 35,000 restaurants worldwide, with the most recent 2025 industry data estimating an annual $9.2 billion in United States system-wide sales. Subway remains the largest sandwich chain in the US, both in location count and estimated sales — but size isn't the whole picture. Its US footprint has fallen from more than 27,000 locations in 2015 to fewer than 19,000 today, with more than 700 closures in 2025 alone. Subway's domestic location count has declined every year since its 2015 peak (though it has seen international growth). In April 2024, Subway was sold to Roark Capital — a private equity firm that also has a large stake in sandwich-chain competitor Jimmy John's — for a reported $9.6 billion. Meanwhile, Jersey Mike's made headlines in July 2026 after announcing plans to go public. It hit the New York Stock Exchange with a $1 billion IPO, one of the largest restaurant-sector debuts in recent years. The New Jersey-founded sandwich chain now operates more than 3,300 locations across the US and Canada. Earlier this year, the chain also announced plans to expand into Europe by opening hundreds of locations across the UK and Ireland. By comparison, in 2015, it had just over 1,000 total locations. Jersey Mike's financials track with its physical growth. In 2025, it posted more than $4 billion in US system-wide sales, a major feat for a chain that has far fewer locations than Subway yet has become one of its top competitors. With all the buzz, I wanted to see which chain actually had better-tasting sandwiches and offered more value to customers. To do so, I ordered a similar cold club sandwich, hot Philly cheesesteak, and chocolate-chip cookie at each, sticking to the chain's regular size and default preparations. Here's how they stacked up. Walking in, the first thing I noticed was a wall decal that read, "It's not a real Jersey Mike's Sub without 'the juice,'" which I learned is a blend of oil and red-wine vinegar. It's one of the chain's specialties. The "Mike's Way" preparation is another signature touch: finishing sandwiches with lettuce, onion, tomato, and "the juice." Fans of the chain also tout its hearty portions and freshly sliced meats and cheeses. Customers can watch staff slice cold cuts with the large metal tools right behind the counter. I hadn't been to Subway since college, so I forgot the chain is basically a design-your-own sandwich bar. The customization aspect is a major highlight, with rows of metal containers filled with veggies, meats, dressings, and cheeses. Subway is also known for its freshly baked bread and offers multiple varieties to choose from — hence why the stores always smell divine. Don't get me wrong, Jersey Mike's menu had plenty of subs and cheesesteaks — especially the latter, with unique flavors like bacon ranch and Buffalo chicken. But for anything beyond a sandwich, or a sandwich-turned-bowl-or-wrap, you may want to look elsewhere. I ordered a 7-inch Club Sub prepared Mike's Way (the default for cold sandwiches), a 7-inch Mike's Famous Philly, and a chocolate-chip cookie for $10.80, $10.40, and $1.50, respectively. My total came to $22.70 before tax. In addition to subs and cheesesteaks, Subway offered pizza, nachos, and breakfast sandwiches, plus lighter and more health-forward options like salads, bowls, and protein pockets. Salads usually call my name, but this time, I was on a mission. To match my Jersey Mike's meal, I picked a 6-inch American Club Sub, a 6-inch Steak Philly, and a chocolate-chip cookie. Each sandwich cost $8.49 and the cookie $0.99, so I paid $17.97 total before tax. Unrolling the oil-and-vinegar-stained paper, I held a bulky sandwich loaded with provolone cheese, ham, turkey, onion, lettuce, tomato, and bacon. The bread, slathered in mayonnaise, oil, vinegar, and oregano, felt pillowy with a crusty edge. Beautiful, yes, but I was skeptical about a wet sandwich. After taking a bite, however, I officially understood the hype. "The juice" gave the bread some tang, and miraculously, it didn't make it soggy. Better yet, the cheese was creamy and the deli meat relatively moist. Slices seemed individually stacked, not stuck together, so I could tell they were freshly cut. Perhaps the best part was the equal proportions of ingredients, or the oregano that rounded out the flavors. Unfortunately, the lettuce hung limp from "the juice," but given all the pros, I could forgive it. Following Jersey Mike's heaping sandwich almost felt unfair, but Subway's All-American Club held its own — for the most part. It contained the same ingredients, minus the oil, vinegar, and spices; instead of provolone cheese, it had American. Subway's club sandwich had a smoky flavor, thanks to the ham and bacon. I appreciated the crunch from the bacon, onions, and lettuce, as well as the generous amount of American cheese. However, the bread wasn't as soft as I'd expected, given Subway's reputation. In fact, it almost felt stale. The turkey also missed the mark for me. I uncovered two thin slices, and they had little flavor and a dry texture. The ham had more taste, but it wasn't juicy, either. My other qualm: The chain went way overboard on the mayonnaise. I wrongly assumed the cheesesteak would be as hefty as the club. It wasn't nearly as substantial. To its credit, the hot sub contained sliced steak, grilled onions, grilled red peppers, and white American cheese, all with outstanding flavor. The steak had a nice tender bite. It also had a solid meat-to-bread ratio, but the sandwich lost points in my book for the bread itself, which was too crusty. Additionally, I felt it needed another slice of cheese. In my opinion, Mike's cheesesteak was just OK. Subway's Steak Philly came with steak, American cheese, green peppers, red onions, and mayonnaise. Now, not everyone will agree, but I didn't enjoy mayo on my cheesesteak — especially since the chain put so much of it. In the future, I'd probably order most of my Subway sandwiches sans mayo. In this cheesesteak from Subway, the green peppers and red onions were left raw, so they were all I tasted. With the crunchy veggies and heaping globs of mayo, it felt less like a cheesesteak and more like a steak sandwich. And with almost no cheese, it didn't have the melty element I craved. A few bites were enough for me. A prepackaged cookie didn't pique my interest, but I wanted to end the meal with something sweet. I'm glad I did. Jersey Mike's chewy cookie had the fudgy, almost underbaked texture I love. Thick and dense with large chocolate pieces, it reminded me of Costco's Kirkland Signature cookies. (If you know, you know.) However, at 3 ¼ inches and $1.50, it was smaller and pricier than Subway's. At only $0.99, Subway's 4-inch chocolate-chip cookie proved hard to beat, and I liked that it came from the bakery case rather than a plastic bag. It had a sweet, buttery flavor and tons of chocolate chips. The texture was light, delicate, and melt-in-your-mouth soft. It hit the spot for a thinner cookie, especially with its ever-so-crisp edges. Even though my club sandwich was pricier at Jersey Mike's versus Subway, it still felt like a better value. And to be fair, I got an extra inch in length at Jersey Mike's, too. Compared to Subway's club, Jersey Mike's had juicier meat, softer bread, and more balanced proportions. Plus, the Mike's Way preparation gave it a subtle Italian flair that paired nicely with the salted meats. Even though I wasn't the biggest fan of Jersey Mike's Philly cheesesteak, I still enjoyed it more than Subway's. That said, I wouldn't order either again. The chocolate-chip cookies were a draw for me. Subway's cookie was incredibly tasty, plus it was bigger and less expensive, but I also enjoyed Jersey Mike's. I'd get both again in a heartbeat. In the end, the so-called "best" depends on your personal taste, your real-time appetite, and what you're willing to pay. For non-sandwich items, healthier-sounding options, and lower prices, Subway delivered. For sandwiches overall, Jersey Mike's edged out the competition. In my opinion, Jersey Mike's biggest drawback was its somewhat limited menu — and the messiness of the sandwiches. Since the Club Sub ended up being my favorite, however, I let it slide. It was worth it for "the juice." When reached for comment, a spokesperson for Subway said, "For over 60 years, Subway has been built on customization. While we offer standard builds, every freshly made sandwich can be tailored to a guest's preferences, from adding extra cheese and protein to swapping veggies and adjusting condiments. We celebrate our guests' individual tastes and encourage them to make each meal their own." Business Insider reached out to Jersey Mike's for comment. No comments right now, check back later. Sections An almost unparalleled example in the history of industrial capitalism MILAN â Half a millennium of gunmaking and fifteen generations â with the sixteenth already coming onto the scene â of fathers passing the company on to their sons. Berettaâs landmark anniversary â exactly 500 years since the contract of 3 October 1526, when master gunsmith Bartolomeo Beretta received 296 ducats to supply 185 arquebus barrels to the Arsenal of the Venetian Republic â is not, in fact, a real birthday. The 16th-century workshop must already have been well established to secure an order of that size from La Serenissima, meaning the story goes back even further. But the exact date matters only so much. What does matter is that the gunmaker in Gardone Val Trompia, in the province of Brescia, has now been in business for more than half a millennium and remains in the hands of Bartolomeoâs descendants: an almost unparalleled example in the history of industrial capitalism, undoubtedly the result of generations of entrepreneurial skill, but perhaps also of making a product for which demand has never seemed to falter.     The iron mines of Val Trompia For a moment, though, it is worth forgetting about pistols, rifles and ammunition and looking instead at the factory itself. Because behind Beretta, and all around it, lies first and foremost its home territory. Centuries ago, Val Trompia already had iron mines, timber to fuel its foundries and, above all, the waters of the River Mella to power production. By the 16th century, manufacturing was organised through a network of specialised workshops, family ties and guilds stretching from Gardone towards Brescia along the river. There was no modern factory yet, but there was already an industrial district, a division of labour and a wealth of skills that economists would much later call know-how. Master Bartolomeo Beretta was part of this world. His descendants would remain part of it for centuries, straddling the line between high-end craftsmanship and an industrial district that was not yet truly industrial, until Pietro Antonio Beretta shaped the modern company in the 19th century and, in 1832, registered the name Fabbrica dâArmi Pietro Beretta. His son Giuseppe Antonio accelerated the modernisation process, introducing new machinery, bringing previously scattered stages of production under one roof and pushing into international markets.     The First World War It was only the first of many transformations. After all, no company survives for 500 years without changing. At the beginning of the 20th century, Pietro Beretta modernised the factory further. Semi-automatic pistols and military production arrived, alongside firearms for civilian use. During the First World War â unsurprisingly â orders soared. The 1930s brought new government contracts and mass production. The war in Ethiopia and, later, the Italian intervention in Spain, were tragedies for those who suffered them, but good business for those making the weapons used on those battlefields. It is hardly surprising, then, that 1945 marked the darkest moment in the companyâs recent history. Orders collapsed, the peace settlement imposed severe restrictions on Italyâs arms industry, and the factories in Gardone suddenly found themselves with too many workers and too much production capacity. In 1946, the Brescia arms industry as a whole employed around 6,500 people, with between 40 and 50 per cent of the workforce considered surplus to production needs. Beretta and Bernardelli, the two companies forming the industrial backbone of the district, were temporarily placed under Allied supervision.     The venture into cars It was at this point that even the Beretta family tried to make a virtue of necessity. In 1948, Giuseppe Pietro Beretta, Giuseppe Benelli and Count Guglielmo Castelbarco Albani filed two patents for a car. The project was called the BBC: a four-seater with a 750cc engine capable of reaching 100 kilometres per hour. It was designed for the affordable car market that Fiat would conquer a few years later with the 600 and the 500. Three BBC prototypes were built between 1948 and 1949. Then the project went no further than that. Legend has it that the order to stop came directly from Turin; more likely, the leap into car manufacturing simply proved too complex and expensive. Beretta instead focused on Mi-Val, founded in the Brescia area by Ettore Minganti, a Bolognese industrialist with close ties to Fascism. The company produced motorcycles, machine tools and even a microcar, the Mivalino, and remained in business until the 1960s. The gunmaking dynasty also invested alongside the US company Underwood in a project to manufacture office equipment. That venture fared no better: the investment was short-lived, and in 1959 a majority stake passed to Olivetti.     Small specialist manufacturers In the end, the most successful diversification was the least adventurous: returning to skills accumulated over centuries and adapting them to a different market. The Brescia district shifted towards civilian and sporting firearms. Around its larger companies, a constellation of small specialist manufacturers re-emerged. Beretta and Bernardelli became the hubs of a decentralised, flexible but hierarchical system in which skills, manufacturing processes and expertise circulated throughout the area. For Beretta, this also meant retaining capabilities that could be put back to use in the military sector when military demand returned. Contracts with NATO armies Italyâs entry into NATO in 1949 reopened opportunities, and in the years that followed the company secured contracts with the armed forces of NATO member countries and manufactured the M1 Garand semi-automatic rifle under US licence. That contract also had an industrial impact. Tighter tolerances and the requirement for fully interchangeable components forced Beretta to upgrade both its machinery and the organisation of its production.     Business in the US The next decisive transformation came in 1985, with the contract that changed both the scale of the company and the international standing of the brand. Beretta won the competition to supply the new standard-issue pistol for the US armed forces, beating American names including Colt and Smith & Wesson. The total order would eventually amount to 600,000 pistols: excellent business in itself, but above all a seal of approval with worldwide value . Beretta Holding was established in 1994, and the family began building a truly multinational group around the original company through acquisitions and a growing portfolio of brands. Today, the 16th-century workshop has become a group generating revenues of â¬1.68 billion and employing more than 6,000 people. Yet the Fabbrica dâArmi Beretta in Gardone remains the symbolic heart of the story. In 2025, it recorded revenues of â¬336 million, and in 2026 it is aiming for â¬350 million. It is also where the two sides of Berettaâs production coexist. On one side are connected machine tools, predictive maintenance, micron-level quality controls and production lines that can operate across three shifts. On the other are individually selected pieces of wood, chequerers and engravers who can spend up to 1,000 hours decorating a single firearm destined for the hands of a multimillionaire who can afford to go hunting with a piece worth a fortune. Mass production and luxury are the two paths that now coexist, apparently without too much contradiction. The Beretta that is raising the stakes in the US by acquiring a 25 per cent stake in rival Sturm, Ruger & Co., strengthening its position in the worldâs largest firearms market, is the same company that also sells country-chic clothing in wool, linen and cashmere. Five hundred years of history are also a powerful way to build a brand. The translation of this article was reviewed by a Language Service Provider GEDI News Network S.p.A. Apple’s current iPad, the A16 model, has gone untouched for well over a year. It remains the only device in Apple’s core product lineup without support for Apple Intelligence. Rumors had swirled for quite some time about an A18 model coming this year. Now, it’s sounding like Apple has an even bigger plan. It’s likely safe to assume that the delays with this product launch have much to do with the ongoing memory crisis affecting the electronics industry. It wouldn’t surprise me if Apple had the A18 refresh roadmapped for earlier this year alongside the debut of the M4 iPad Air, then had to push it. As a reminder, Apple raised the price of the base iPad from $349 to $449 this summer alongside the rest of its memory-related price hikes. This brings it back to the price it initially launched at in 2022. However, a new leak from MacRumors contributor Aaron Perris paints a more promising picture. Instead of utilizing the A18 chip, it sounds like the next entry-level iPad will equip the A19 chip. Alongside that, you’ll get the N1 networking chip, as well as the C1X modem on the cellular version. This’ll bring support for Wi-Fi 7 to Apple’s cheapest iPad. The A19 iPad will also be equipped with 8GB of memory, allowing users to run Siri AI, though you’ll still miss out on the most capable local models and the more advanced dictation models, as those features require 12GB of memory. It’s not a major loss, but worth pointing out. Another possibility is that the A19 iPad might offer a new name. With the debut of the MacBook Neo, Apple marketing exec Greg Joswiak pointed out that calling the MacBook Neo just “MacBook” would leave it without an identity. Hopefully, with the next entry-level iPad, we also get some sort of proper name like “SE” or “Neo” so we have something to call it. Beyond that, don’t expect any sort of redesign or display improvements. There may be new colors, but probably nothing else. I personally wish Apple would bring USB 3 to the product, so users don’t have to suffer with such slow transfer speeds. It’d certainly help justify the new higher starting price. The iPad is just… I wish they would increase the display refresh rate. The budget version – 90Hz, Air – 120Hz, Pro – 144Hz or higher. Something like that. As for the chipset, I always say this, but it has always been top-notch in the tablet lineup, so it’s still more than enough now. Apple’s next budget iPad should be releasing next Spring, per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. That’ll accompany other products like the M6 MacBook Air, A19 Pro MacBook Neo, M7 14-inch MacBook Pro, and more. Are you someone in the market for the entry-level iPad? What are you most looking forward to? Let us know in the comments. The Shropshire Astronomical Society said the dome would look similar to this one A group of amateur astronomers have been given permission to set up a mini-observatory at a village hall. Members of the Shropshire Astronomical Society (SAS) now plan to transfer over the out of use dome and telescope once used by the Irish Rangers at the Tern Hill army base near Market Drayton. They have been based at Rodington Village Hall, near Shrewsbury, for 25 years but think the telescope will raise interest in astronomy. In granting permission, Telford and Wrekin planners said the curved gloss white fibreglass dome used to house the telescope would be "somewhat unusual" but would add "some visual interest to the site. In the group's application, the society's Stephen Szwajkun wrote: "It will be a first public astronomical observatory in the area and provide inspiration for the diverse residents of Telford and Wrekin as well as the wider area." Society chairman Philip Osman said a permanent observatory would encourage participation and also give the group the opportunity to organise community outreach activities. "The dome will be the only publicly accessible observatory in the county and we hope that this new facility will allow us to broaden our outreach activities and successfully engage with a new generation," he said. Osman also said an agreement had been reached to purchase the mini observatory in May. The domed structure is set to be a little less than 2.7m (8ft 9inches) tall and council officials were satisfied that the proposal would not result in unacceptable noise, disturbance or any other disruption for nearby residents. They added that it was "not considered likely to result in a significant increase in traffic or parking demand". Planners agreed that it would provide a useful additional community and educational facility. This news was gathered by the Local Democracy Reporting Service which covers councils and other public service organisations. Nina Totenberg                        Broadcast journalists work in front of the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 15. The new term begins on Monday.                                                           Roberto Schmidt/AFP via Getty Images                                       hide caption  The U.S. Supreme Court formally opens a new term on Monday, with big test cases on religion, bans on semi-automatic weapons, climate change, immigration and — waiting in the wings — election law cases. It used to be that the first Monday in October marked the beginning of a new Supreme Court term. And that's still true, technically. But for all practical purposes, the formerly quiet summer months after the court finishes its opinions in all argued cases no longer exists. Indeed, as Georgetown University law professor Stephen Vladeck observes, the number of emergency appeals has ballooned during the Trump administration, while at the same time, fully briefed and argued cases have dropped precipitously over the years. "So now we have twice as many full court rulings on emergency applications as we have on the merits docket," Vladeck observes, adding, "That is a very new phenomenon." The difference is that decisions on the emergency docket are rendered quickly, with little briefing, no oral arguments, and ultimately little or no explanation of the ruling. In contrast, a decision on the merits is typically worked on for months after full briefing and lengthy oral arguments. Of late, the court seems to be making an effort to offer some limited explanations of its emergency docket rulings, but lower court judges, both liberal and conservative, complain that isn't enough to provide them with adequate guidance. And the Trump administration often takes what used to be the rare step of getting to the Supreme Court by leapfrogging over lower appellate courts that the administration views as hostile. With that backdrop, here are the cases the court will be hearing in the coming weeks: Climate change The opening case, to be argued Monday, tests whether state and local governments can sue energy companies for allegedly deceiving the public about the damaging effects of fossil fuels. "The theory is that the energy company defendants deceived the public for many years," says Deepak Gupta, who teaches at Harvard Law School and practices law in Washington, D.C. What the companies were telling the public for years, he says, is "the opposite of what the company's own scientists knew, and the local cost of that deception." That said, however, most court observers see the case as an uphill battle for environmentalists. Religion Perhaps the biggest case of the term so far, in terms of ripple effects, involves religion, a subject on which the court's conservative super majority has dramatically changed its legal doctrine. Indeed for the better part of a century, the Supreme Court emphasized the First Amendment's separation of church and state, with the free exercise of religion playing an important — but secondary — role. Since President Trump's appointment of three new justices, however, things have changed. "It's literally the opposite of what the law was not that long ago, and it's just a complete shift," observes Michigan State University law professor Frank Ravitch. The court may, in fact, be on the verge of requiring taxpayers to fund religious schools that refuse to admit LGBTQ students and parents. Last term the justices deadlocked on the issue in a separate case after Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused herself because of a conflict. The 4-4 tie vote automatically left in place an Oklahoma Supreme Court decision that barred overtly religious charter schools from from being funded by the taxpayers. But this year the issue is back in a case from Colorado. The case centers on a state law that provides universal preschool programs that are open to all students, regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation or gender identity. St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colo., wants the state funding guaranteed in the state's universal pre-k law. But it doesn't want to admit LGBTQ students or students with gay or trans parents. The parish maintains such admissions would violate church's right to the free exercise of religion. The state counters that funding the church school would violate the state's anti-discrimination law. The court's conservative majority has, in multiple cases, ruled in favor of religious exemptions from generally applicable laws. Until now, however, the court has never said that religious schools are entitled to full taxpayer funding. But given the current court's views, and with Justice Barrett participating in the Colorado case, taxpayers could well end up having to fund religious schools in Colorado and elsewhere. Bans on semi-automatic weapons In December the court will hear a case testing whether state and local governments violate the Second Amendment right to bear arms when they ban semi-automatic weapons, like the AR-15. Former Solicitor General Don Verrilli Jr., articulates two different ways to look at the question. On the one hand the AR-15 "can deliver upwards of 100 bullets per minute" without any enhancements, and 500 bullets per minute with various enhancements. On the other hand, he notes that millions of Americans own AR-15s, "and it would be quite disruptive to suggest all these Americans ... would be dispossessed of their weapons." Lawyer Erin Murphy, who has litigated lots of cases on behalf of gun owners, says the "single most important question is who gets to decide what guns you have," and he argues it makes no sense to say, "You've got this right against the government, but the government decides which arms you can get." Immigration The Trump administration has repeatedly taken positions in immigration cases that no other administration has adopted. Most recently, the court announced it would hear arguments and decide a case testing whether the Department of Homeland Security may deport migrants to so-called "third countries," when their countries of origin refuse to accept them. Since Trump began his second term, his administration has deported thousands of people to third world countries where they have no connections, may not speak the language, have often been jailed and allegedly subject to torture. The court has twice blocked lower court decisions that prevented the third country policy, and now the justices have said they will hear arguments about the policy in December.  In a second immigration case, the issue is the Trump administration's policy of detaining undocumented immigrants without a bond hearing, regardless of how long they have been in the U.S. Possible cases: The 10 commandments and much more  There are many more cases waiting in the wings that the justices may take up. Among them is a case that seeks to reverse a nearly half-century-old Supreme Court precedent; it bars public schools from posting the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms. Now, however, Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana and Alabama have passed laws that conflict with the Supreme Court's 1980 ruling, and the lower courts are split on the question. That split all but guarantees the the Supreme Court will revisit the question. Another case that could to make it to the court this term tests whether states can regulate Kalshi, the $40 billion prediction market behemoth that has sports fans betting on everything from the next pitch to the point spread or at the other end of the spectrum, betting on the outcome of Supreme Court cases. And then there are cases that the Trump administration has slow-walked for close to two years, after quickly losing in the lower courts. Prime examples are the administration's attempt to deny medical research grants to Harvard University, and other attempts to deny security clearances to law firms, as well as seeking money damages from law firms Trump views as hostile. Earlier this year the Justice Department told a federal court in Washington that it was dropping the law firm cases. But the next day it went back to court to reverse course. "They don't want to take up cases that they're going to lose, but on the other hand, they have a boss who wants everything taken up there [to the Supreme Court]," says Stanford University law professor Pam Karlan. Georgetown's professor Vladeck adds that in his view, "The real story of the upcoming term hasn't been written yet because what we're going to look back on as the biggest cases of the term … are not on the docket yet." Elections More immediately, the probability is that like it or not the justices will be drawn into the election. The Trump administration has sought to influence elections in numerous ways, and it's unclear what efforts the administration might take going forward.  Democrats have a battalion of lawyers lined up to deal with problems on the ground — whether it's moving polling places at the last minute or having federal agents stationed near polling places. But if there are serious voting problems, they will likely end up at the Supreme Court's door — on the emergency docket. NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. In the Gilmore Girls fandom, we often dream of visiting the idyllic town of Stars Hollow, Connecticut, just as the leaves change hue. We could stop in for a cup of coffee at Luke's Diner, read classic literature under the shade of a tree at the park, and watch the town prep for the fall festival on the green, under the watchful eye of Taylor Doose. Too bad it's all fictional, right? Fortunately, it turns out that it isn't completely fiction. While Stars Hollow and its specific quirks were created for the TV series, the cozy, small-town charm was inspired by a real place. Even the Independence Inn and the Dragonfly Inn were based on an inn that actually exists. Amy Sherman-Palladino created Gilmore Girls after a trip to Washington, Connecticut, and fell in love with all the real autumnal comforts the Northeastern town offered. Before Gilmore Girls was even a glimmer in their eye, Sherman-Palladino and her husband, Dan Palladino, were taking a vacation across the country from their California home. They flew to New York and planned to drive through Connecticut. Sherman-Palladino said she wanted to visit Mark Twain's house in Hartford, Connecticut, to get design and decor inspiration. The couple booked a stay at the Mayflower Inn in Washington, Connecticut, and that's when the ideas began flowing. Washington, Connecticut, was a completely different world from what Sherman-Palladino knew in California. She was amazed at the friendly, welcoming atmosphere, with people stopping to chat as they walked through town. While eating at a local diner, she watched a regular get his own coffee when the waitress was busy. The wheels spun in her mind as she said to herself, "If I can make people feel this much of what I felt walking around this fairy town, I thought that would be wonderful." It wasn't just the overall vibe of a small-town fall season in Washington, Connecticut, that inspired Sherman-Palladino. Several places in Stars Hollow directly correlate to buildings in and around the real-life town. Luke's Diner is a mix of Marty's CafÃ© and The Po CafÃ©, both located in or near the center of town, Washington Depot. The Mayflower Inn and Spa became the basis for the Independence Inn, where Lorelai (Lauren Graham) worked in the early seasons of the show. The Washington Food Market is similar to Doose's Market, Hickory Stick Books is the real-life Stars Hollow Books, and Titus Park and Garage is just like Gypsy's. All of these places gave Sherman-Palladino so much inspiration that she had already begun planning her series, even writing some of the pilot's dialogue, during her trip. Washington isn't the only town in Litchfield County, Connecticut, to have the same cozy feel as Stars Hollow. If you're looking for a gazebo on the town green, New Milford is the perfect spot. Woodbury is a real town that Taylor (Michael Winters) sees as a rival to Stars Hollow, and many of his revamps are to stay in competition with Woodbury. We might not be able to visit Stars Hollow, but a trip to these Connecticut towns or the others in the area will feel as if you've actually stepped into the world that the famous Gilmore duo inhabit. It was thanks to the vacation that Amy Sherman-Palladino took, almost thirty years ago, that Gilmore Girls came to be, and fans will be forever grateful to those towns for the inspiration. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. GoPro is responsible for the rise of the action camera market and is still one of the most popular action camera brands today. Its products, like the latest GoPro Mission 1 Pro, are able to capture great photos under the most adventurous conditions. But do you remember when GoPro made drones? The GoPro Karma drone launched in 2016 and was discontinued in 2018, with no successor ever to be seen. In an interview with TechCrunch, GoPro CEO Nick Woodman revealed exactly why the company stopped making drones. There was a disastrous "domino effect" for the company resulting from the poor sales of the Hero5 Black action camera that was also released in 2016. "If Hero5 Black had sold to expectations at its original $399 pricing, we would not have had to change prices across all of our cameras, and we would not have had to do a restructuring and we would have been able to continue investing in programs like our next generation Karma," Woodman explained. His reference to a restructuring was a gentle way of phrasing the situation; GoPro laid off over 250 positions — one-fifth of its workforce at the time — back in 2018 following the catastrophic situation surrounding the Karma drone. GoPro's history is full of soaring highs and terrifying lows. In June 2026, GoPro (link will download a PDF to your device) warned its investors that there was "substantial doubt about the company's ability to continue" following a period of poor finances and another round of massive layoffs. With conditions like this being relatively common for the company, it makes sense that it wouldn't risk another shot at the drone market. The GoPro Karma drone is a touchstone example of an overhyped tech gadget that failed on arrival, and its circumstances dealt a long-lasting blow to the company. Another Karma controversy could quite possibly put GoPro in the grave once and for all. On the other hand, things are looking up for GoPro after talks of a fruitful merger with Starman Optical and the release of a promising new lineup of products. Travelers and outdoor adventurers still love using GoPro products — so much so that there's a wide range of useful accessories that GoPro owners swear by. If positive factors continue to align, maybe GoPro could succeed at breaking into the drone market after all.
