Google’s original Pixel Fold was inherently flawed but also fundamentally way better than I expected and, thanks to recent arrivals, also way ahead of its time. Foldables were still very much going through growing pains in 2023 when Google stepped up to the plate with its first foldable, the Pixel Fold. At the time, I called it “better than it should be, but far from perfect,” and I stand by that. Even with hindsight of three more Google foldables and the rapid improvements of the rest of the industry, the Pixel Fold managed to do a lot right at the time. It offered sturdy hardware, respectable cameras, and less compromises than most other foldables of the time. Has it aged well? Not particularly. The glossy finish to the metal frame remains a fingerprint magnet in the worst kind of way, and the sheer heft of this phone is wild. I don’t often take issue with a heavy smartphone, but especially compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 I’ve been using the past couple of months, the original Pixel Fold is noticeably heavy in the hand. The crease down the center is huge, and it’s a thick device too. And, three years later, I can only imagine how bad Tensor G2’s heat management issues have become – that was ultimately the deal-breaker for me when I was using the device last.  Yet, for everything it got wrong, the Pixel Fold got one thing right, the form factor. In the wake of Apple’s debut in the foldable market, brands are quickly pivoting to wider form factors, and they seem to be resonating with customers. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a smash hit, and I bet we’ll be seeing a lot more of these wide foldables over the next year.  But the Pixel Fold did it three years ago, albeit with a lot less flash.  Google’s foldable looks almost normal compared to a Galaxy Z Fold 8, but the core idea is the same. The wider canvas is designed for better multitasking and tablet apps, something that I pointed out in my original review. Where Samsung’s foldables were really good at using phone apps on a bigger canvas, the Pixel Fold was far more likely to trigger a proper tablet version of an app instead.  After around two decades using Google services and products (wow I feel old), I have to say that's just typical Google, they're among the first, have a great idea, make some mistakes, abandon it, re-release after someone succesfully polish their idea...  I won't say it happens every single time, but it's frequent enough that is kind of disheartening. I suspect that's why I have a love/hate relationship with them. Google ultimately threw that away. Why? Android apps simply weren’t ready at the time. While Android apps have always been designed around scaling to form factors, bigger and wider canvases were still in the minority, and most apps didn’t fully support them. As such, the taller and squarish design just made more sense. Arguably, it still does, but Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 has shown that it works when you do it “right.” Two months into using it, I’m thrilled with this form factor, and a bit annoyed that Google gave up on it so quickly even though, at the time, it probably made sense. Unfortunately, that’s a bit of a trend in the Pixel’s legacy and Google’s as a whole – Inbox, Stadia, etc. It doesn’t take much to find a Google idea that was left behind too quickly. It’s anyone’s guess when Google might revisit this design, but I hope it happens.  Follow Ben: Twitter/X, Threads, Bluesky, and Instagram FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More. Photo: Ikenna Obianeri  Kindly share this story: The Anambra State Government has ordered the immediate closure of Otuocha Company Market following renewed violence between Aguleri and Umuoba-Anam communities in Anambra East Local Government Area. The violence, which erupted amid a land dispute between the two communities, left five people dead, with several others injured and properties, including the palace of the traditional ruler of Aguleri, burnt. The palace was set ablaze late on Friday by unknown persons following an exchange of gunfire in the area. The fresh violence occurred shortly after a team led by the state Commissioner of Police, Nnanna Oji, and the Deputy Governor, Onyekachukwu Ibezim, visited the communities for an on-the-spot assessment.  During the visit, several houses, shops, a rice processing factory containing numerous bags of rice and other properties were found burnt, while traders reportedly fled the area with their remaining goods. Residents alleged that the crisis was triggered by Aguleri Community’s attempt to erect a signpost and install Closed-Circuit Television cameras at the boundary between the two communities, which was opposed by Umuoba-Anam. Following the renewed violence, Ibezim, who is also the Chairman of the Anambra State Boundary Committee, announced the closure of the market on the instruction of Governor Chukwuma Soludo.         He said the market would remain closed until the government concluded its assessment of the damage and investigations into the incident.See more Punch stories on Google.Add Punch on Google “The market will remain shut until further notice to allow the state government to ascertain the level of damage caused by the crisis. “And no activity will take place there until the state government completes necessary investigations and takes appropriate action against those responsible for the incident. “No community leader or local government chairman has the authority to determine boundaries between communities without the knowledge of the state government. The State Boundary Committee is responsible for the monumentation of boundaries within the state,” he said. Some sections of the market were set ablaze. Photo: Ikenna Obianeri Speaking in separate interviews, the traditional rulers of Aguleri and Umuoba-Anam, Igwe Michael Idigo and Igwe George Ekwealor, respectively, said the dispute escalated after Aguleri people attempted to erect a signpost and security cameras in the market area. They also said several people were hospitalised and property was destroyed during the clash.      The traditional rulers commended the state government for its intervention, saying it helped prevent further casualties and destruction. Meanwhile, the Anambra State Police Command condemned the renewed violence and alleged arson in the area. In a statement on Saturday, the command’s spokesman, SP Tochukwu Ikenga, said the fresh violence was a breach of the peace agreement reached after the earlier intervention by security and government officials. Ikenga said, “The Command strongly condemns the resort to violence, destruction of property and other acts capable of undermining the prevailing peace and security in the affected communities. “The Command reiterates its commitment to maintaining law and order, while it commends community leaders, government officials, security stakeholders and residents who have continued to adhere to the agreed peace resolution and refrain from actions capable of escalating the situation. “The peaceful resolution of disputes remains the most responsible path to sustainable peace and development. “We urge all parties to exercise restraint and allow ongoing engagements and lawful processes to address their grievances.”         Ikenga warned that anyone found culpable after investigation would face prosecution. “The Command also calls on traditional rulers, town union leaders, youth leaders, women’s groups and other stakeholders in both communities to continue to work with the Police and other security agencies in sustaining calm and preventing further escalation,” the statement added. He urged residents to remain vigilant and provide credible information about persons or groups planning to disrupt the peace through appropriate security channels.
